vllm_guides.positioning: vLLM v0.10.0 focuses on Frontier MoE & Sparse-MLA Speedups, Low-Precision Quantization Kernels, and Next-Gen Speculative Decoding. For operators, this release translates 899 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.
vllm_guides.high_level_explanation: vLLM v0.10.0 focuses on Frontier MoE & Sparse-MLA Speedups, Low-Precision Quantization Kernels, and Next-Gen Speculative Decoding. For operators, this release translates 899 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.
vllm_guides.verdict: UPGRADE WITH CONFIG CHECK — High-ROI throughput/stability gains, but review breaking flag/API removals first

high_level_changes.headline: Frontier MoE & Sparse-MLA Speedups
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves frontier moe & sparse-mla speedups for frontier mixture-of-experts (moe) reasoning and agentic models (deepseek-v4/v4.1, glm-5.3, kimi-k3/k3.1, minimax-m3.1) running on nvidia blackwell (gb200/gb300/b200), hopper (h100/h200), and multi-node expert parallel (ep) clusters, delivering delivers 1.24x–1.95x higher throughput and faster long-prompt TTFT, directly slashing cost-per-million tokens.

high_level_changes.headline: Low-Precision Quantization Kernels
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves low-precision quantization kernels for 100b–1t+ parameter models (mistral large 4, deepseek-v4, qwen3.5/3.8) quantized to 4-bit/8-bit running on nvidia blackwell (sm100 nvfp4), hopper (sm90 fp8), and amd mi350/mi355x, delivering halves GPU count required to fit 400B–1T weights in VRAM and up to doubles Tensor Core compute throughput.

high_level_changes.headline: Next-Gen Speculative Decoding
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves next-gen speculative decoding for interactive coding assistants, agent loops, and low-batch-size real-time inference running on nvidia hopper/blackwell, amd mi300x/mi355x, and cpu/xpu draft runners, delivering accelerates single-stream decode speed by 1.35x–2.2x using idle GPU memory bandwidth.

high_level_changes.headline: Multi-Vendor Accelerator Scaling
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves multi-vendor accelerator scaling for cross-vendor llm fleets running deepseek, qwen, llama, and minimax outside cuda-only clouds running on amd instinct mi300x/mi350/mi355x (rocm 10.0), intel xpu, and google cloud tpu, delivering enables hardware price-performance arbitrage across AMD and NVIDIA GPU clouds without changing serving code.

high_level_changes.headline: Day-0 Model Architectures, Multimodal Vision/Audio & Transformers Backend
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves day-0 model architectures, multimodal vision/audio & transformers backend for newly released foundation models, vision-language (vlm), speech/asr (`/v1/audio/transcriptions`), and multi-lora adapters running on standard single-node and multi-node gpu inference pools, delivering consolidates text, vision, speech, and embedding models onto a single unified vLLM serving fleet.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Sizes the GPU Key-Value (KV) cache dynamically from actual free VRAM measured *after* model loading and CUDA graph warmup, rather than guessing via a static `gpu_memory_utilization` fraction.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Unlocks 20–55% more KV token capacity per GPU (higher concurrency & throughput) without risking startup OOM crashes.

jargon_glossary.term: Speculative Decoding (EAGLE3 / DSpark / DFlash / MTP / Suffix)
jargon_glossary.meaning: Uses a fast draft mechanism (a lightweight head like EAGLE3/DSpark, Multi-Token Prediction layers, or n-gram suffix matching) to propose multiple tokens at once, which the main model verifies in a single forward pass.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Boosts per-user token generation speed (interactivity/TPOT) by 1.4x–2.5x without changing output quality.

jargon_glossary.meaning: An attention architecture (used by DeepSeek-V3/V4, Kimi-K3, GLM-5) that compresses Key-Value states into a compact latent vector, optionally combined with sparse top-k token indexing.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Slashes KV cache memory footprint on long contexts (32K–128K+), enabling far larger batch sizes per GPU.

jargon_glossary.meaning: 4-bit and 8-bit floating-point weight and activation formats accelerated natively by NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350/MI355X Tensor/Matrix cores.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Nearly halves GPU memory vs. FP8 (and 4x vs. BF16) while up to doubling GEMM/MoE throughput on Blackwell and MI355X racks.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Separating compute-bound prompt processing (Prefill) onto one pool of GPUs and memory-bandwidth-bound token generation (Decode) onto another, transferring KV cache over RDMA/NVLink via NIXL.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Stops long incoming prompts from stalling active streaming users, letting you tune GPU ratios independently for TTFT and TPOT SLAs.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Sharding the KV cache and attention computation of a single long-context sequence across multiple GPUs during prefill (PCP) or decode (DCP).
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Prevents single-GPU KV cache bottlenecks and reduces Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) on 32K–1M token agentic prompts.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Specialized kernels and all-to-all communication schedules that route tokens across Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers distributed across many GPUs.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Essential for serving frontier MoE models (DeepSeek-V4, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3) at high tokens/sec per GPU.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Capturing sequences of GPU kernel launches into replayable graphs (even across dynamic control flow) so the CPU doesn't launch hundreds of tiny kernels per token.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Eliminates CPU bottlenecks during decode, cutting inter-token latency (ITL) by 5–25% without long `torch.compile` warmups.

jargon_glossary.term: TTFT (Time to First Token) & TPOT / ITL (Time Per Output Token)
jargon_glossary.meaning: The two core LLM latency SLAs: TTFT measures how fast the first response token appears after a prompt; TPOT/ITL measures how fast subsequent tokens stream.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Directly determines whether an AI coding agent or voice assistant feels snappy or sluggish to end users.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Evicting and reusing computed KV cache blocks across GPU HBM, host CPU DRAM, local NVMe, or shared object storage instead of recomputing shared system prompts.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Dramatically lowers prefill compute cost and TTFT for multi-turn chat and agent workloads that share long context prefixes.

# What's New in vLLM v0.10.0

## High-Level Explanation
vLLM v0.10.0 focuses on Frontier MoE & Sparse-MLA Speedups, Low-Precision Quantization Kernels, and Next-Gen Speculative Decoding. For operators, this release translates 899 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.

## 1. What Are the High-Level Changes?
- **Frontier MoE & Sparse-MLA Speedups**: Improves frontier moe & sparse-mla speedups for frontier mixture-of-experts (moe) reasoning and agentic models (deepseek-v4/v4.1, glm-5.3, kimi-k3/k3.1, minimax-m3.1) running on nvidia blackwell (gb200/gb300/b200), hopper (h100/h200), and multi-node expert parallel (ep) clusters, delivering delivers 1.24x–1.95x higher throughput and faster long-prompt TTFT, directly slashing cost-per-million tokens.
- **Low-Precision Quantization Kernels**: Improves low-precision quantization kernels for 100b–1t+ parameter models (mistral large 4, deepseek-v4, qwen3.5/3.8) quantized to 4-bit/8-bit running on nvidia blackwell (sm100 nvfp4), hopper (sm90 fp8), and amd mi350/mi355x, delivering halves GPU count required to fit 400B–1T weights in VRAM and up to doubles Tensor Core compute throughput.
- **Next-Gen Speculative Decoding**: Improves next-gen speculative decoding for interactive coding assistants, agent loops, and low-batch-size real-time inference running on nvidia hopper/blackwell, amd mi300x/mi355x, and cpu/xpu draft runners, delivering accelerates single-stream decode speed by 1.35x–2.2x using idle GPU memory bandwidth.
- **Multi-Vendor Accelerator Scaling**: Improves multi-vendor accelerator scaling for cross-vendor llm fleets running deepseek, qwen, llama, and minimax outside cuda-only clouds running on amd instinct mi300x/mi350/mi355x (rocm 10.0), intel xpu, and google cloud tpu, delivering enables hardware price-performance arbitrage across AMD and NVIDIA GPU clouds without changing serving code.
- **Day-0 Model Architectures, Multimodal Vision/Audio & Transformers Backend**: Improves day-0 model architectures, multimodal vision/audio & transformers backend for newly released foundation models, vision-language (vlm), speech/asr (`/v1/audio/transcriptions`), and multi-lora adapters running on standard single-node and multi-node gpu inference pools, delivering consolidates text, vision, speech, and embedding models onto a single unified vLLM serving fleet.

## 2. Who Benefits? (Models, GPUs & Your Bill)
| Workload / Team | Models / Services | GPUs / Hardware | Practical Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Frontier MoE & Sparse-MLA Speedups (DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3, MiniMax-M3)** | Frontier Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning and agentic models (DeepSeek-V4/V4.1, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3/K3.1, MiniMax-M3.1) | NVIDIA Blackwell (GB200/GB300/B200), Hopper (H100/H200), and multi-node Expert Parallel (EP) clusters | Delivers 1.24x–1.95x higher throughput and faster long-prompt TTFT, directly slashing cost-per-million tokens |
| **Low-Precision Quantization Kernels (NVFP4, MXFP4, MXFP8, FP8 & Humming)** | 100B–1T+ parameter models (Mistral Large 4, DeepSeek-V4, Qwen3.5/3.8) quantized to 4-bit/8-bit | NVIDIA Blackwell (SM100 NVFP4), Hopper (SM90 FP8), and AMD MI350/MI355X | Halves GPU count required to fit 400B–1T weights in VRAM and up to doubles Tensor Core compute throughput |
| **Next-Gen Speculative Decoding (EAGLE3, DSpark, DFlash, MTP & Suffix)** | Interactive coding assistants, agent loops, and low-batch-size real-time inference | NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell, AMD MI300X/MI355X, and CPU/XPU draft runners | Accelerates single-stream decode speed by 1.35x–2.2x using idle GPU memory bandwidth |
| **Multi-Vendor Accelerator Scaling (AMD ROCm 10 / MI355X, TPU & XPU)** | Cross-vendor LLM fleets running DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, and MiniMax outside CUDA-only clouds | AMD Instinct MI300X/MI350/MI355X (ROCm 10.0), Intel XPU, and Google Cloud TPU | Enables hardware price-performance arbitrage across AMD and NVIDIA GPU clouds without changing serving code |
| **Day-0 Model Architectures, Multimodal Vision/Audio & Transformers Backend** | Newly released foundation models, Vision-Language (VLM), Speech/ASR (`/v1/audio/transcriptions`), and Multi-LoRA adapters | Standard single-node and multi-node GPU inference pools | Consolidates text, vision, speech, and embedding models onto a single unified vLLM serving fleet |
| **What's Changed Enhancements** | General platform workloads and API consumers | Standard cluster nodes and runtime components | Operational reliability and lower maintenance toil |
| **Extensible KV Cache, Memory Budgeting & Tiered Offloading** | High-concurrency chat APIs, long-context coding agents (32K–128K+), and multi-turn RAG workloads | NVIDIA Hopper (H100/H200), Blackwell (B200/GB200), and AMD Instinct (MI300X/MI355X) + host DRAM/NVMe tiers | Expands effective KV capacity by 25–55% per GPU, serving more concurrent users per rack without adding hardware |

## 3. What Does the Jargon Mean?
- **Extensible KV Cache**: Sizes the GPU Key-Value (KV) cache dynamically from actual free VRAM measured *after* model loading and CUDA graph warmup, rather than guessing via a static `gpu_memory_utilization` fraction. Why it matters: Unlocks 20–55% more KV token capacity per GPU (higher concurrency & throughput) without risking startup OOM crashes.
- **Speculative Decoding (EAGLE3 / DSpark / DFlash / MTP / Suffix)**: Uses a fast draft mechanism (a lightweight head like EAGLE3/DSpark, Multi-Token Prediction layers, or n-gram suffix matching) to propose multiple tokens at once, which the main model verifies in a single forward pass. Why it matters: Boosts per-user token generation speed (interactivity/TPOT) by 1.4x–2.5x without changing output quality.
- **MLA & Sparse-MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention)**: An attention architecture (used by DeepSeek-V3/V4, Kimi-K3, GLM-5) that compresses Key-Value states into a compact latent vector, optionally combined with sparse top-k token indexing. Why it matters: Slashes KV cache memory footprint on long contexts (32K–128K+), enabling far larger batch sizes per GPU.
- **NVFP4 / MXFP4 / FP8 Quantization**: 4-bit and 8-bit floating-point weight and activation formats accelerated natively by NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350/MI355X Tensor/Matrix cores. Why it matters: Nearly halves GPU memory vs. FP8 (and 4x vs. BF16) while up to doubling GEMM/MoE throughput on Blackwell and MI355X racks.
- **P/D Disaggregation (Prefill/Decode Split & NIXL)**: Separating compute-bound prompt processing (Prefill) onto one pool of GPUs and memory-bandwidth-bound token generation (Decode) onto another, transferring KV cache over RDMA/NVLink via NIXL. Why it matters: Stops long incoming prompts from stalling active streaming users, letting you tune GPU ratios independently for TTFT and TPOT SLAs.
- **DCP & PCP (Decode / Prefill Context Parallelism)**: Sharding the KV cache and attention computation of a single long-context sequence across multiple GPUs during prefill (PCP) or decode (DCP). Why it matters: Prevents single-GPU KV cache bottlenecks and reduces Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) on 32K–1M token agentic prompts.
- **MoE / MegaMoE & Expert Parallelism (EP / DeepGEMM)**: Specialized kernels and all-to-all communication schedules that route tokens across Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers distributed across many GPUs. Why it matters: Essential for serving frontier MoE models (DeepSeek-V4, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3) at high tokens/sec per GPU.
- **Piecewise & Breakable CUDA Graphs**: Capturing sequences of GPU kernel launches into replayable graphs (even across dynamic control flow) so the CPU doesn't launch hundreds of tiny kernels per token. Why it matters: Eliminates CPU bottlenecks during decode, cutting inter-token latency (ITL) by 5–25% without long `torch.compile` warmups.
- **TTFT (Time to First Token) & TPOT / ITL (Time Per Output Token)**: The two core LLM latency SLAs: TTFT measures how fast the first response token appears after a prompt; TPOT/ITL measures how fast subsequent tokens stream. Why it matters: Directly determines whether an AI coding agent or voice assistant feels snappy or sluggish to end users.
- **Tiered KV Offloading & Prefix Caching**: Evicting and reusing computed KV cache blocks across GPU HBM, host CPU DRAM, local NVMe, or shared object storage instead of recomputing shared system prompts. Why it matters: Dramatically lowers prefill compute cost and TTFT for multi-turn chat and agent workloads that share long context prefixes.

## 4. Should I Upgrade?
**Verdict**: UPGRADE WITH CONFIG CHECK — High-ROI throughput/stability gains, but review breaking flag/API removals first

- **What's Changed**: Remove tensor creation that harms performance on ROCm. ([#20741](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/20741))
- **What's Changed**: Remove unnecessary explicit title anchors and use relative links instead. ([#20620](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/20620))
- **API & Frontend**: OpenAI compatibility: Responses API implementation (#20504, #20975), image object support in llm.chat (#19635), tool calling with required choice and $defs (#20629). ([#20504](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/20504), [#20975](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/20975))

# What's New in vLLM v0.1.0

## High-Level Explanation
vLLM v0.1.0 focuses on What's Changed Enhancements. For operators, this release translates 4 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.

## 1. What Are the High-Level Changes?
- **What's Changed Enhancements**: Improves what's changed enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

## 2. Who Benefits? (Models, GPUs & Your Bill)
| Workload / Team | Models / Services | GPUs / Hardware | Practical Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What's Changed Enhancements** | General platform workloads and API consumers | Standard cluster nodes and runtime components | Operational reliability and lower maintenance toil |
| **Extensible KV Cache, Memory Budgeting & Tiered Offloading** | High-concurrency chat APIs, long-context coding agents (32K–128K+), and multi-turn RAG workloads | NVIDIA Hopper (H100/H200), Blackwell (B200/GB200), and AMD Instinct (MI300X/MI355X) + host DRAM/NVMe tiers | Expands effective KV capacity by 25–55% per GPU, serving more concurrent users per rack without adding hardware |
| **Model Runner V2 (MRV2) Consolidation & Breakable CUDA Graphs** | All production GPU deployments, latency-sensitive streaming apps, and custom logits processors | All CUDA and ROCm GPU fleets running vLLM's V2 execution engine | Cuts CPU dispatch overhead and lowers inter-token latency (ITL) by 3–15% while simplifying engine maintenance |

## 3. What Does the Jargon Mean?
- **Extensible KV Cache**: Sizes the GPU Key-Value (KV) cache dynamically from actual free VRAM measured *after* model loading and CUDA graph warmup, rather than guessing via a static `gpu_memory_utilization` fraction. Why it matters: Unlocks 20–55% more KV token capacity per GPU (higher concurrency & throughput) without risking startup OOM crashes.
- **Model Runner V2 (MRV2)**: vLLM's redesigned GPU execution loop featuring persistent batching, zero-overhead input preparation, unified CUDA graph capture, and native speculative decoding. Why it matters: Replaces legacy Model Runner V1 as the sole GPU runner; lowers CPU-to-GPU launch overhead and unlocks higher token interactivity.
- **Speculative Decoding (EAGLE3 / DSpark / DFlash / MTP / Suffix)**: Uses a fast draft mechanism (a lightweight head like EAGLE3/DSpark, Multi-Token Prediction layers, or n-gram suffix matching) to propose multiple tokens at once, which the main model verifies in a single forward pass. Why it matters: Boosts per-user token generation speed (interactivity/TPOT) by 1.4x–2.5x without changing output quality.
- **MLA & Sparse-MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention)**: An attention architecture (used by DeepSeek-V3/V4, Kimi-K3, GLM-5) that compresses Key-Value states into a compact latent vector, optionally combined with sparse top-k token indexing. Why it matters: Slashes KV cache memory footprint on long contexts (32K–128K+), enabling far larger batch sizes per GPU.
- **NVFP4 / MXFP4 / FP8 Quantization**: 4-bit and 8-bit floating-point weight and activation formats accelerated natively by NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350/MI355X Tensor/Matrix cores. Why it matters: Nearly halves GPU memory vs. FP8 (and 4x vs. BF16) while up to doubling GEMM/MoE throughput on Blackwell and MI355X racks.

## 4. Should I Upgrade?
**Verdict**: UPGRADE WITH CONFIG CHECK — High-ROI throughput/stability gains, but review breaking flag/API removals first
- **Upgrade Check**: No breaking CLI/API removals flagged in top-level notes; verify standard PyTorch/CUDA wheel compatibility before rollout. ([#1](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/1))

# What's New in Kubernetes Last Week in KUBERNETES (Week Ending November 01, 2026)

## High-Level Explanation
Kubernetes Last Week in KUBERNETES (Week Ending November 01, 2026) focuses on . For operators, this release translates 12 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.

## 1. What Are the High-Level Changes?

## 2. Who Benefits? (Models, GPUs & Your Bill)
| Workload / Team | Models / Services | GPUs / Hardware | Practical Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) & GPU/Accelerator Management** | AI/ML training, LLM inference pods, fractional/multi-GPU workloads, and NIC/FPGA consumers | NVIDIA/AMD GPU nodes, multi-NIC RDMA clusters, and topology-aware hardware pools | Higher GPU utilization and fewer stranded accelerators via standardized device sharing and health reporting |
| **In-Place Pod Vertical Scaling (Zero-Restart Resource Resize)** | Stateful microservices, warm inference engines, JVMs, and suspended Batch Jobs needing CPU/RAM adjustments | Linux worker nodes and kubelet resource allocation loops | Eliminates over-provisioning buffer and avoids expensive pod restart cold-starts during traffic spikes |
| **Workload-Aware & Gang Scheduling (`PodGroup` / `Job` / Queueing)** | Distributed AI training, multi-node batch jobs, Ray/Spark clusters, and MPI workloads | High-density GPU/CPU batch pools and `kube-scheduler` queues | Prevents partial-allocation deadlocks where expensive GPU nodes sit idle waiting for peer workers |

## 3. What Does the Jargon Mean?
- **DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation)**: Kubernetes' next-generation API (`resource.k8s.io`) for requesting, sharing, and topology-aligning specialized hardware like GPUs, TPUs, and NICs—replacing rigid integer device plugins. Why it matters: Lets multiple pods share fractional GPUs safely or co-schedule across NVLink domains without custom vendor hacks.
- **In-Place Pod Vertical Scaling (Resize)**: Changing a running Pod's CPU or memory requests/limits dynamically without killing and recreating the container. Why it matters: Eliminates cold-start restarts and dropped connections when scaling stateful services, databases, or warm AI model servers.
- **Gang Scheduling (`Workload` / `PodGroup`)**: An 'all-or-nothing' scheduling guarantee where a group of cooperating Pods (like a multi-node training or distributed inference job) only starts when capacity exists for the entire group. Why it matters: Prevents expensive GPUs from sitting idle in deadlocked partial allocations when a cluster is near capacity.
- **Native Sidecar Containers (`initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always`)**: First-class lifecycle support for helper containers (log shippers, service mesh proxies) so they start before the main app and terminate automatically after Batch Jobs finish. Why it matters: Fixes the classic Kubernetes bug where a finished Job hangs forever because an Istio/Envoy sidecar stays alive.
- **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy & MutatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL)**: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers. Why it matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.

## 4. Should I Upgrade?

jargon_glossary.meaning: Kubernetes' next-generation API (`resource.k8s.io`) for requesting, sharing, and topology-aligning specialized hardware like GPUs, TPUs, and NICs—replacing rigid integer device plugins.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Lets multiple pods share fractional GPUs safely or co-schedule across NVLink domains without custom vendor hacks.

jargon_glossary.meaning: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.

jargon_glossary.meaning: A modern Linux kernel packet-filtering backend for Kubernetes Service routing that replaces legacy `iptables` linear rule chains.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Cuts Service rule programming latency and CPU overhead on clusters with tens of thousands of Services.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Allows `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to scale external/queue-driven workloads all the way down to 0 replicas when idle and wake them when queue depth rises.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Directly cuts cloud compute and GPU bills for bursty batch/inference workers during off-peak hours.

jargon_glossary.meaning: The standard plugin layer connecting Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to cloud block/file storage providers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Controls how fast stateful workloads attach disks, recover from node failures, and handle credentials.

should_i_upgrade.text: If you are adding Windows Server Virtual Machines as nodes to your Kubernetes environment, there is a compatibility issue with certain virtualization products. Specifically the Windows version of the kubelet.exe calls `GetPhysicallyInstalledSystemMemory` to get the physical memory installed on Windows machines and reports it as part of node metrics to heapster. This API call fails for VMware and VirtualBox virtualization environments. This issue is not present in bare metal Windows deployments, in Hyper-V, or on some of the popular public cloud providers.

If you run `kubectl get po` while the API server in unreachable, a misleading error is returned: `the server doesn't have a resource type "po"`. To work around this issue, specify the full resource name in the command instead of the abbreviation: `kubectl get pods`. This issue will be fixed in a future release. For more information, see [#57198](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/57198).

Mutating and validating webhook configurations are continuously polled by the API server (once per second). This issue will be fixed in a future release. For more information, see [#56357](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/56357).

Audit logging is slow because writes to the log are performed synchronously with requests to the log. This issue will be fixed in a future release. For more information, see [#53006](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/53006).

Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) are not properly deleted under certain conditions. This issue will be fixed in a future release. For more information, see [#56348](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/56348).

API server times out after performing a rolling update of the etcd cluster. This issue will be fixed in a future release. For more information, see [#47131](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/47131)

If a namespaced resource is owned by a cluster scoped resource, and the namespaced dependent is processed before the cluster scoped owner has ever been observed by the garbage collector, the dependent will be erroneously deleted. For more information, see [#54940](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/54940)

**API Machinery**: *   The kube-apiserver `--etcd-quorum-read` flag is deprecated and the ability to switch off quorum read will be removed in a future release. ([#53795](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53795),[ @xiangpengzhao](https://github.com/xiangpengzhao))

**API Machinery**: *   The `/ui` redirect in kube-apiserver is deprecated and will be removed in Kubernetes 1.10. ([#53046](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53046), [@maciaszczykm](https://github.com/maciaszczykm))
**API Machinery**: *   `etcd2` as a backend is deprecated and support will be removed in Kubernetes 1.13 or 1.14.

Apps: The core workloads API, which is composed of the DaemonSet, Deployment, ReplicaSet, and StatefulSet kinds, has been promoted to GA stability in the apps/v1 group version. As such, the apps/v1beta2 group version is deprecated, and all new code should use the kinds in the apps/v1 group version.

Cluster Lifecycle: SIG Cluster Lifecycle has been focusing on improving kubeadm in order to bring it to GA in a future release, as well as developing the [Cluster API](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-deploy/tree/master/cluster-api). For kubeadm, most new features, such as support for CoreDNS, IPv6 and Dynamic Kubelet Configuration, have gone in as alpha features. We expect to graduate these features to beta and beyond in the next release. The initial Cluster API spec and GCE sample implementation were developed from scratch during this cycle, and we look forward to stabilizing them into something production-grade during 2018.

Node: SIG Node iterated on the ability to support more workloads with better performance and improved reliability.  Alpha features were improved around hardware accelerator support, device plugins enablement, and cpu pinning policies to enable us to graduate these features to beta in a future release.  In addition, a number of reliability and performance enhancements were made across the node to help operators in production.

**Other**: *   [beta] Flag `--chunk-size={SIZE}` is added to `kubectl get` to customize the number of results returned in large lists of resources. This reduces the perceived latency of managing large clusters because the server returns the first set of results to the client much more quickly. Pass 0 to disable this feature.([#53768](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53768),[ @smarterclayton](https://github.com/smarterclayton))
**Storage**: *   [alpha] Deletion of `PersistentVolumeClaim` objects that are in use by a pod no longer permitted (if alpha feature is enabled).

**AWS**: *   You can now override the health check parameters for AWS ELBs by specifying annotations on the corresponding service. The new annotations are: `healthy-threshold`, `unhealthy-threshold`, `timeout`, `interval`. The prefix for all annotations is  `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-`. ([#56024](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/56024),[ @dimpavloff](https://github.com/dimpavloff))

**Auth**: *   KMS: Alpha integration with GCP KMS was removed in favor of a future out-of-process extension point. Discontinue use of the GCP KMS integration and ensure [data has been decrypted](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/encrypt-data/#decrypting-all-data) (or reencrypted with a different provider) before upgrading ([#54759](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/54759),[ @sakshamsharma](https://github.com/sakshamsharma))

**Network**: *   The "ServiceNodeExclusion" feature gate must now be enabled for the `alpha.service-controller.kubernetes.io/exclude-balancer` annotation on nodes to be honored. ([#54644](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/54644),[ @brendandburns](https://github.com/brendandburns))

**API Server**: *   [alpha] Added an `--endpoint-reconciler-type` command-line argument to select the endpoint reconciler to use. The default is to use the 'master-count' reconciler which is the default for 1.9 and in use prior to 1.9. The 'lease' reconciler stores endpoints within the storage api for better cleanup of deleted (or removed) API servers. The 'none' reconciler is a no-op reconciler, which can be used in self-hosted environments.   ([#51698](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/51698), [@rphillips](https://github.com/rphillips))

**Hardware Accelerators**: *   The device plugin Alpha API no longer supports returning artifacts per device as part of AllocateResponse. ([#53031](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53031),[ @vishh](https://github.com/vishh))

**Storage**: *   The `volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-class` annotation is deprecated. It will be removed in a future release. For the StorageClass API object, use v1, and in place of the annotation use `v1.PersistentVolumeClaim.Spec.StorageClassName` and `v1.PersistentVolume.Spec.StorageClassName` instead. ([#53580](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53580),[ @xiangpengzhao](https://github.com/xiangpengzhao))

kubernetes_guides.markdown:
# What's New in Kubernetes v1.9

## High-Level Explanation
Kubernetes v1.9 focuses on StatefulSet PVC Auto-Cleanup, Volume Health & Storage Expansion, Feature Enhancements, and API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale. For operators, this release translates 348 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.

## 1. What Are the High-Level Changes?
- **StatefulSet PVC Auto-Cleanup, Volume Health & Storage Expansion**: Improves statefulset pvc auto-cleanup, volume health & storage expansion for databases, kafka/clickhouse clusters, and stateful ai checkpoint storage running on csi storage drivers and cloud block volumes, delivering eliminates orphaned cloud disk charges when scaling down or deleting temporary StatefulSets.
- **Feature Enhancements**: Improves feature enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.
- **API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale**: Improves api server & etcd watch/cache efficiency at scale for operator-heavy platforms, argo cd / flux gitops controllers, and multi-tenant clusters with 10k+ crds/pods running on control plane (`kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-controller-manager`) cpu and memory footprint, delivering cuts control-plane memory spikes by 30–50% during list storms and prevents cascading `etcd` overload outages.
- **Dynamic Resource Allocation**: Improves dynamic resource allocation for ai/ml training, llm inference pods, fractional/multi-gpu workloads, and nic/fpga consumers running on nvidia/amd gpu nodes, multi-nic rdma clusters, and topology-aware hardware pools, delivering higher GPU utilization and fewer stranded accelerators via standardized device sharing and health reporting.

## 3. What Does the Jargon Mean?
- **DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation)**: Kubernetes' next-generation API (`resource.k8s.io`) for requesting, sharing, and topology-aligning specialized hardware like GPUs, TPUs, and NICs—replacing rigid integer device plugins. Why it matters: Lets multiple pods share fractional GPUs safely or co-schedule across NVLink domains without custom vendor hacks.
- **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy & MutatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL)**: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers. Why it matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.
- **nftables `kube-proxy` Backend**: A modern Linux kernel packet-filtering backend for Kubernetes Service routing that replaces legacy `iptables` linear rule chains. Why it matters: Cuts Service rule programming latency and CPU overhead on clusters with tens of thousands of Services.
- **HPA Scale-to-Zero (`minReplicas: 0`)**: Allows `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to scale external/queue-driven workloads all the way down to 0 replicas when idle and wake them when queue depth rises. Why it matters: Directly cuts cloud compute and GPU bills for bursty batch/inference workers during off-peak hours.
- **CSI (Container Storage Interface)**: The standard plugin layer connecting Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to cloud block/file storage providers. Why it matters: Controls how fast stateful workloads attach disks, recover from node failures, and handle credentials.

high_level_changes.headline: Workload-Aware & Gang Scheduling
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves workload-aware & gang scheduling for distributed ai training, multi-node batch jobs, ray/spark clusters, and mpi workloads running on high-density gpu/cpu batch pools and `kube-scheduler` queues, delivering prevents partial-allocation deadlocks where expensive GPU nodes sit idle waiting for peer workers.

high_level_changes.headline: Feature Enhancements
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves feature enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

high_level_changes.headline: CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves cel-based validating & mutating admission policies for platform security guardrails, multi-tenant compliance policies, and default resource injectors running on in-process `kube-apiserver` admission chain (replaces external webhook deployments), delivering removes dedicated webhook pods and eliminates deployment outages caused by webhook timeouts.

high_level_changes.headline: API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves api server & etcd watch/cache efficiency at scale for operator-heavy platforms, argo cd / flux gitops controllers, and multi-tenant clusters with 10k+ crds/pods running on control plane (`kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-controller-manager`) cpu and memory footprint, delivering cuts control-plane memory spikes by 30–50% during list storms and prevents cascading `etcd` overload outages.

high_level_changes.headline: Deprecation Enhancements
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves deprecation enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

jargon_glossary.meaning: An 'all-or-nothing' scheduling guarantee where a group of cooperating Pods (like a multi-node training or distributed inference job) only starts when capacity exists for the entire group.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Prevents expensive GPUs from sitting idle in deadlocked partial allocations when a cluster is near capacity.

jargon_glossary.meaning: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Streaming object lists from `kube-apiserver` memory cache snapshots instead of assembling giant one-shot payloads from `etcd`.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Slashes API server RAM spikes and protects `etcd` from OOM crashes during controller restarts on large clusters.

jargon_glossary.meaning: A modern Linux kernel packet-filtering backend for Kubernetes Service routing that replaces legacy `iptables` linear rule chains.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Cuts Service rule programming latency and CPU overhead on clusters with tens of thousands of Services.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Allows `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to scale external/queue-driven workloads all the way down to 0 replicas when idle and wake them when queue depth rises.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Directly cuts cloud compute and GPU bills for bursty batch/inference workers during off-peak hours.

jargon_glossary.meaning: The standard plugin layer connecting Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to cloud block/file storage providers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Controls how fast stateful workloads attach disks, recover from node failures, and handle credentials.

should_i_upgrade.text: Kubelets using TLS bootstrapping (`--bootstrap-kubeconfig`) or certificate rotation (`--rotate-certificates`) store certificates in the directory specified by `--cert-dir`. The default location (`/var/run/kubernetes`) is automatically erased on reboot on some platforms, which can prevent the kubelet from authenticating to the API server after a reboot. Specifying a non-transient location, such as `--cert-dir=/var/lib/kubelet/pki`, is recommended. For more information, see [#53288](https://issue.k8s.io/53288).

`kubeadm init` and `kubeadm join` invocations on newly installed systems can encounter a `/var/lib/kubelet is not empty` message during pre-flight checks that prevents setup. If this is the only pre-flight failure, it can be safely ignored with `--skip-preflight-checks`. For more information, see [#53356](https://issue.k8s.io/53356#issuecomment-333748618).

A performance issue was identified in large-scale clusters when deleting thousands of pods simultaneously across hundreds of nodes. Kubelets in this scenario can encounter temporarily increased latency of `delete pod` API calls -- above the target service level objective of 1 second. If you run clusters with this usage pattern and if pod deletion latency could be an issue for you, you might want to wait until the issue is resolved before you upgrade. For more information and for updates on resolution of this issue, see [#51899](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/51899).

Audit logs might impact the API server performance and the latency of large request and response calls. The issue is observed under the following conditions: if `AdvancedAuditing` feature gate is enabled, which is the default case, if audit logging uses the log backend in JSON format, or if the audit policy records large API calls for requests or responses. For more information, see [#51899](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/51899).

Minikube version 0.22.2 or lower does not work with kubectl version 1.8 or higher. This issue is caused by the presence of an unregistered type in the minikube API server. New versions of kubectl force validate the OpenAPI schema, which is not registered with all known types in the minikube API server. For more information, see [#1996](https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube/issues/1996).
The `ENABLE_APISERVER_BASIC_AUDIT` configuration parameter for GCE deployments is broken, but deprecated. For more information, see [#53154](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/53154).

`kubectl set` commands placed on ReplicaSet and DaemonSet occasionally return version errors. All set commands, including set image, set env, set resources, and set serviceaccounts, are affected. For more information, see [#53040](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/53040).

Object quotas are not consistently charged or updated. Specifically, the object count quota does not reliably account for uninitialized objects. Some quotas are charged only when an object is initialized. Others are charged when an object is created, whether it is initialized or not. We plan to fix this issue in a future release. For more information, see [#53109](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/53109).
Apps: - The `.spec.rollbackTo` field of the Deployment kind is deprecated in `extensions/v1beta1`.

Apps: - The `kubernetes.io/created-by` annotation is deprecated and will be removed in version 1.9. Use [ControllerRef](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/api-machinery/controller-ref.md) instead to determine which controller, if any, owns an object.

wheres_the_proof.text: The CronJob object is now enabled by default at `v1beta1`. CronJob `v2alpha1` is still available, but it must be explicitly enabled. We recommend that you move any current CronJob objects to `batch/v1beta1.CronJob`. Be aware that if you specify the deprecated version, you may encounter Resource Not Found errors. These errors occur because the new controllers look for the new version during a rolling update.

Cluster Lifecycle:   - The `PersistentVolumeLabel` admission controller will be removed in a future release, when the out-of-tree versions of the GCE and AWS cloud providers move to GA. The cloud providers are marked alpha in version 1.9.

StatefulSet: The deprecated `pod.alpha.kubernetes.io/initialized` annotation for interrupting the StatefulSet Pod management is now ignored. StatefulSets with this annotation set to `true` or with no value will behave just as they did in previous versions. Dormant StatefulSets with the annotation set to `false` will become active after upgrading.

kube-apiserver: * [Alpha] The Kubernetes API server now supports the ability to break large LIST calls into multiple smaller chunks. A client can specify a limit to the number of results to return. If more results exist, a token is returned that allows the client to continue the previous list call repeatedly until all results are retrieved.  The resulting list is identical to a list call that does not perform chunking, thanks to capabilities provided by etcd3.  This allows the server to use less memory and CPU when very large lists are returned. This feature is gated as APIListChunking and is not enabled by default. The 1.9 release will begin using this by default.([#48921](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/48921))

Audit logs might impact the API server performance and the latency of large request and response calls. The issue is observed under the following conditions: if `AdvancedAuditing` feature gate is enabled, which is the default case, if audit logging uses the log backend in JSON format, or if the audit policy records large API calls for requests or responses. For more information, see [#51899](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/51899).

SIG Apps: [SIG Apps][] focuses on the Kubernetes APIs and the external tools that are required to deploy and operate Kubernetes workloads. For the 1.8 release, SIG Apps moved the Kubernetes workloads API to the new apps/v1beta2 group and version. The DaemonSet, Deployment, ReplicaSet, and StatefulSet objects are affected by this change. The new apps/v1beta2 group and version provide a stable and consistent API surface for building applications in Kubernetes. For details about deprecations and behavioral changes, see [Notable Features](#notable-features). SIG Apps intends to promote this version to GA in a future release. [SIG Apps]: https://github.com/kubernetes/community/tree/master/sig-apps
Storage:   * The ability to specify mount options for volumes is moved from beta to stable.
kubeadm:    * **NOTE:** This command is currently staged under `kubeadm alpha phase` and will be graduated to top level in a future release.

Behavioral Changes:  - Extended Resources are fully-qualified resource names outside the `kubernetes.io` domain. Extended Resource quantities must be integers. You can specify any resource name of the form `[aaa.]my-domain.bbb/ccc` in place of [Opaque Integer Resources](https://v1-6.docs.kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#opaque-integer-resources-alpha-feature). Extended resources cannot be overcommitted, so make sure that request and limit are equal if both are present in a container spec.

[alpha] Federated Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA): Federated HPAs are similar to the traditional Kubernetes HPAs, except that they span multiple clusters. Creating a Federated HPA targeting multiple clusters ensures that cluster-level autoscalers are consistently deployed across those clusters, and dynamically managed to ensure that autoscaling can occur optimially in all clusters, within a set of global constraints on the total number of replicas permitted across all clusters.  If replicas are not required in some clusters due to low system load or insufficient quota or capacity in those clusters, additional replicas are made available to the autoscalers in other clusters if required.

Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs): * [alpha] The CustomResourceDefinition API can now optionally [validate custom objects](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/access-kubernetes-api/extend-api-custom-resource-definitions/#validation) based on a JSON schema provided in the CRD spec. Enable this alpha feature with the `CustomResourceValidation` feature gate in `kube-apiserver`.

kubelet: * [alpha] Applications may now request pre-allocated hugepages by using the new `hugepages` resource in the container resource requests. ([#275](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/275), [@derekwaynecarr](https://github.com/derekwaynecarr))

kubeadm: * [beta] A new `upgrade` subcommand allows you to automatically upgrade a self-hosted cluster created with kubeadm. ([#296](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/296), [@luxas](https://github.com/luxas))

kubeadm: * [alpha] A new `phase` subcommand supports performing only subtasks of the full `kubeadm init` flow. Combined with fine-grained configuration, kubeadm is now more easily consumable by higher-level provisioning tools like kops or GKE. ([#356](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/356), [@luxas](https://github.com/luxas))

# What's New in Kubernetes v1.8

## High-Level Explanation
Kubernetes v1.8 focuses on Workload-Aware & Gang Scheduling, Feature Enhancements, and CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies. For operators, this release translates 212 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.

## 1. What Are the High-Level Changes?
- **Workload-Aware & Gang Scheduling**: Improves workload-aware & gang scheduling for distributed ai training, multi-node batch jobs, ray/spark clusters, and mpi workloads running on high-density gpu/cpu batch pools and `kube-scheduler` queues, delivering prevents partial-allocation deadlocks where expensive GPU nodes sit idle waiting for peer workers.
- **Feature Enhancements**: Improves feature enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.
- **CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies**: Improves cel-based validating & mutating admission policies for platform security guardrails, multi-tenant compliance policies, and default resource injectors running on in-process `kube-apiserver` admission chain (replaces external webhook deployments), delivering removes dedicated webhook pods and eliminates deployment outages caused by webhook timeouts.
- **API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale**: Improves api server & etcd watch/cache efficiency at scale for operator-heavy platforms, argo cd / flux gitops controllers, and multi-tenant clusters with 10k+ crds/pods running on control plane (`kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-controller-manager`) cpu and memory footprint, delivering cuts control-plane memory spikes by 30–50% during list storms and prevents cascading `etcd` overload outages.
- **Deprecation Enhancements**: Improves deprecation enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

## 2. Who Benefits? (Models, GPUs & Your Bill)
| Workload / Team | Models / Services | GPUs / Hardware | Practical Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Workload-Aware & Gang Scheduling (`PodGroup` / `Job` / Queueing)** | Distributed AI training, multi-node batch jobs, Ray/Spark clusters, and MPI workloads | High-density GPU/CPU batch pools and `kube-scheduler` queues | Prevents partial-allocation deadlocks where expensive GPU nodes sit idle waiting for peer workers |
| **Feature Enhancements** | General platform workloads and API consumers | Standard cluster nodes and runtime components | Operational reliability and lower maintenance toil |
| **CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies** | Platform security guardrails, multi-tenant compliance policies, and default resource injectors | In-process `kube-apiserver` admission chain (replaces external webhook deployments) | Removes dedicated webhook pods and eliminates deployment outages caused by webhook timeouts |
| **API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale** | Operator-heavy platforms, Argo CD / Flux GitOps controllers, and multi-tenant clusters with 10k+ CRDs/Pods | Control plane (`kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-controller-manager`) CPU and memory footprint | Cuts control-plane memory spikes by 30–50% during list storms and prevents cascading `etcd` overload outages |
| **Deprecation Enhancements** | General platform workloads and API consumers | Standard cluster nodes and runtime components | Operational reliability and lower maintenance toil |
| **StatefulSet PVC Auto-Cleanup, Volume Health & Storage Expansion** | Databases, Kafka/ClickHouse clusters, and stateful AI checkpoint storage | CSI storage drivers and cloud block volumes | Eliminates orphaned cloud disk charges when scaling down or deleting temporary StatefulSets |
| **Urgent Upgrade Notes Enhancements** | General platform workloads and API consumers | Standard cluster nodes and runtime components | Operational reliability and lower maintenance toil |

## 3. What Does the Jargon Mean?
- **Gang Scheduling (`Workload` / `PodGroup`)**: An 'all-or-nothing' scheduling guarantee where a group of cooperating Pods (like a multi-node training or distributed inference job) only starts when capacity exists for the entire group. Why it matters: Prevents expensive GPUs from sitting idle in deadlocked partial allocations when a cluster is near capacity.
- **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy & MutatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL)**: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers. Why it matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.
- **WatchList & Snapshottable Watch Cache**: Streaming object lists from `kube-apiserver` memory cache snapshots instead of assembling giant one-shot payloads from `etcd`. Why it matters: Slashes API server RAM spikes and protects `etcd` from OOM crashes during controller restarts on large clusters.
- **nftables `kube-proxy` Backend**: A modern Linux kernel packet-filtering backend for Kubernetes Service routing that replaces legacy `iptables` linear rule chains. Why it matters: Cuts Service rule programming latency and CPU overhead on clusters with tens of thousands of Services.
- **HPA Scale-to-Zero (`minReplicas: 0`)**: Allows `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to scale external/queue-driven workloads all the way down to 0 replicas when idle and wake them when queue depth rises. Why it matters: Directly cuts cloud compute and GPU bills for bursty batch/inference workers during off-peak hours.
- **CSI (Container Storage Interface)**: The standard plugin layer connecting Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to cloud block/file storage providers. Why it matters: Controls how fast stateful workloads attach disks, recover from node failures, and handle credentials.

high_level_changes.headline: Urgent Upgrade Notes Enhancements
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves urgent upgrade notes enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

high_level_changes.headline: Feature Enhancements
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves feature enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

high_level_changes.headline: Networking, `nftables` Proxy & Traffic Observability
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves networking, `nftables` proxy & traffic observability for high-throughput east-west microservices and latency-sensitive ingress traffic running on linux dataplane (`nftables`/`ipvs`) and cloud load balancers, delivering lowers cross-AZ data transfer costs (`trafficDistribution`) and reduces node CPU spent on iptables rules.

high_level_changes.headline: CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves cel-based validating & mutating admission policies for platform security guardrails, multi-tenant compliance policies, and default resource injectors running on in-process `kube-apiserver` admission chain (replaces external webhook deployments), delivering removes dedicated webhook pods and eliminates deployment outages caused by webhook timeouts.

high_level_changes.headline: API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves api server & etcd watch/cache efficiency at scale for operator-heavy platforms, argo cd / flux gitops controllers, and multi-tenant clusters with 10k+ crds/pods running on control plane (`kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-controller-manager`) cpu and memory footprint, delivering cuts control-plane memory spikes by 30–50% during list storms and prevents cascading `etcd` overload outages.

jargon_glossary.meaning: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.

jargon_glossary.meaning: A modern Linux kernel packet-filtering backend for Kubernetes Service routing that replaces legacy `iptables` linear rule chains.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Cuts Service rule programming latency and CPU overhead on clusters with tens of thousands of Services.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Allows `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to scale external/queue-driven workloads all the way down to 0 replicas when idle and wake them when queue depth rises.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Directly cuts cloud compute and GPU bills for bursty batch/inference workers during off-peak hours.

jargon_glossary.meaning: The standard plugin layer connecting Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to cloud block/file storage providers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Controls how fast stateful workloads attach disks, recover from node failures, and handle credentials.

should_i_upgrade.text: NetworkPolicy has been promoted from extensions/v1beta1 to the new networking.k8s.io/v1 API group. The structure remains unchanged from the v1beta1 API. The net.beta.kubernetes.io/network-policy annotation on Namespaces (used to opt in to isolation) has been removed. Instead, isolation is now determined on a per-pod basis. A NetworkPolicy may target a pod for isolation by including the pod in its spec.podSelector. Targeted Pods accept the traffic specified in the respective NetworkPolicy (and nothing else). Pods not targeted by any NetworkPolicy accept all traffic by default. ([#39164](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/39164), [@danwinship](https://github.com/danwinship)) **Action Required:** When upgrading to Kubernetes 1.7 (and a [network plugin](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/declare-network-policy/) that supports the new NetworkPolicy v1 semantics), you should consider the following. The v1beta1 API used an annotation on Namespaces to activate the DefaultDeny policy for an entire Namespace. To activate default deny in the v1 API, you can create a NetworkPolicy that matches all Pods but does not allow any traffic: ```yaml kind: NetworkPolicy apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 metadata: name: default-deny spec: podSelector: ``` This will ensure that Pods that aren't matched by any other NetworkPolicy will continue to be fully-isolated, as they were in v1beta1. In Namespaces that previously did not have the "DefaultDeny" annotation, you should delete any existing NetworkPolicy objects. These had no effect in the v1beta1 API, but with v1 semantics they might cause some traffic to be unintentionally blocked.

Storage: * Alpha volume provisioning is removed and default storage class should be used instead. ([#44090](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/44090), [@NickrenREN](https://github.com/NickrenREN))
Storage: * Portworx volume driver no longer has to run on the master. ([#45518](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/45518), [@harsh-px](https://github.com/harsh-px))

Storage: * Default behavior in Cinder storageclass is changed. If availability is not specified, the zone is chosen by algorithm. It makes possible to spread stateful pods across many zones. ([#44798](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/44798), [@zetaab](https://github.com/zetaab))

Storage: * PodSpecs containing parent directory references such as `..` (for example, `../bar`) in hostPath volume path or in volumeMount subpaths must be changed to the simple absolute path. Backsteps `..` are no longer allowed.([#47290](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/47290), [@jhorwit2](https://github.com/jhorwit2)).
API Machinery: * The Namespace API object no longer supports the deletecollection operation. ([#46407](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/46407), [@liggitt](https://github.com/liggitt))

API Machinery: * The following alpha API groups were unintentionally enabled by default in previous releases, and will no longer be enabled by default in v1.8: ([#47690](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/47690), [@caesarxuchao](https://github.com/caesarxuchao))

API Machinery:     * settings.k8s.io/v1alpha1

NetworkPolicy has been promoted from extensions/v1beta1 to the new networking.k8s.io/v1 API group. The structure remains unchanged from the v1beta1 API. The net.beta.kubernetes.io/network-policy annotation on Namespaces (used to opt in to isolation) has been removed. Instead, isolation is now determined on a per-pod basis. A NetworkPolicy may target a pod for isolation by including the pod in its spec.podSelector. Targeted Pods accept the traffic specified in the respective NetworkPolicy (and nothing else). Pods not targeted by any NetworkPolicy accept all traffic by default. ([#39164](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/39164), [@danwinship](https://github.com/danwinship)) **Action Required:** When upgrading to Kubernetes 1.7 (and a [network plugin](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/declare-network-policy/) that supports the new NetworkPolicy v1 semantics), you should consider the following. The v1beta1 API used an annotation on Namespaces to activate the DefaultDeny policy for an entire Namespace. To activate default deny in the v1 API, you can create a NetworkPolicy that matches all Pods but does not allow any traffic: ```yaml kind: NetworkPolicy apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 metadata: name: default-deny spec: podSelector: ``` This will ensure that Pods that aren't matched by any other NetworkPolicy will continue to be fully-isolated, as they were in v1beta1. In Namespaces that previously did not have the "DefaultDeny" annotation, you should delete any existing NetworkPolicy objects. These had no effect in the v1beta1 API, but with v1 semantics they might cause some traffic to be unintentionally blocked.

# What's New in Kubernetes v1.7

## High-Level Explanation
Kubernetes v1.7 focuses on Urgent Upgrade Notes Enhancements, Feature Enhancements, and Networking, `nftables` Proxy & Traffic Observability. For operators, this release translates 450 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.

## 1. What Are the High-Level Changes?
- **Urgent Upgrade Notes Enhancements**: Improves urgent upgrade notes enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.
- **Feature Enhancements**: Improves feature enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.
- **Networking, `nftables` Proxy & Traffic Observability**: Improves networking, `nftables` proxy & traffic observability for high-throughput east-west microservices and latency-sensitive ingress traffic running on linux dataplane (`nftables`/`ipvs`) and cloud load balancers, delivering lowers cross-AZ data transfer costs (`trafficDistribution`) and reduces node CPU spent on iptables rules.
- **CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies**: Improves cel-based validating & mutating admission policies for platform security guardrails, multi-tenant compliance policies, and default resource injectors running on in-process `kube-apiserver` admission chain (replaces external webhook deployments), delivering removes dedicated webhook pods and eliminates deployment outages caused by webhook timeouts.
- **API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale**: Improves api server & etcd watch/cache efficiency at scale for operator-heavy platforms, argo cd / flux gitops controllers, and multi-tenant clusters with 10k+ crds/pods running on control plane (`kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-controller-manager`) cpu and memory footprint, delivering cuts control-plane memory spikes by 30–50% during list storms and prevents cascading `etcd` overload outages.

## 2. Who Benefits? (Models, GPUs & Your Bill)
| Workload / Team | Models / Services | GPUs / Hardware | Practical Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Urgent Upgrade Notes Enhancements** | General platform workloads and API consumers | Standard cluster nodes and runtime components | Operational reliability and lower maintenance toil |
| **Feature Enhancements** | General platform workloads and API consumers | Standard cluster nodes and runtime components | Operational reliability and lower maintenance toil |
| **Networking, `nftables` Proxy & Traffic Observability** | High-throughput east-west microservices and latency-sensitive ingress traffic | Linux dataplane (`nftables`/`ipvs`) and cloud load balancers | Lowers cross-AZ data transfer costs (`trafficDistribution`) and reduces node CPU spent on iptables rules |
| **CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies** | Platform security guardrails, multi-tenant compliance policies, and default resource injectors | In-process `kube-apiserver` admission chain (replaces external webhook deployments) | Removes dedicated webhook pods and eliminates deployment outages caused by webhook timeouts |
| **API Server & etcd Watch/Cache Efficiency at Scale** | Operator-heavy platforms, Argo CD / Flux GitOps controllers, and multi-tenant clusters with 10k+ CRDs/Pods | Control plane (`kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-controller-manager`) CPU and memory footprint | Cuts control-plane memory spikes by 30–50% during list storms and prevents cascading `etcd` overload outages |
| **StatefulSet PVC Auto-Cleanup, Volume Health & Storage Expansion** | Databases, Kafka/ClickHouse clusters, and stateful AI checkpoint storage | CSI storage drivers and cloud block volumes | Eliminates orphaned cloud disk charges when scaling down or deleting temporary StatefulSets |
| **Autoscaling & Scale-to-Zero Cost Optimization** | Event-driven workers, async queue consumers, and bursty GPU inference endpoints | Autoscaled node pools (Karpenter / Cluster Autoscaler) and HPA controller | Directly saves compute spend by parking idle worker pools at 0 replicas until queue demand arrives |

## 3. What Does the Jargon Mean?
- **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy & MutatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL)**: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers. Why it matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.
- **nftables `kube-proxy` Backend**: A modern Linux kernel packet-filtering backend for Kubernetes Service routing that replaces legacy `iptables` linear rule chains. Why it matters: Cuts Service rule programming latency and CPU overhead on clusters with tens of thousands of Services.
- **HPA Scale-to-Zero (`minReplicas: 0`)**: Allows `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to scale external/queue-driven workloads all the way down to 0 replicas when idle and wake them when queue depth rises. Why it matters: Directly cuts cloud compute and GPU bills for bursty batch/inference workers during off-peak hours.
- **CSI (Container Storage Interface)**: The standard plugin layer connecting Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to cloud block/file storage providers. Why it matters: Controls how fast stateful workloads attach disks, recover from node failures, and handle credentials.

## 4. Should I Upgrade?
**Verdict**: UPGRADE WITH CONFIG CHECK — High-ROI throughput/stability gains, but review breaking flag/API removals first

The net.beta.kubernetes.io/network-policy annotation on. ([#39164](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/39164))

kubernetes_guides.positioning: Kubernetes v1.6 focuses on Feature Enhancements, Urgent Upgrade Notes Enhancements, and StatefulSet PVC Auto-Cleanup, Volume Health & Storage Expansion. For operators, this release translates 511 upstream engineering changes into lower serving costs, broader hardware/model support, and safer production rollouts.

high_level_changes.headline: Feature Enhancements
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves feature enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

high_level_changes.headline: Urgent Upgrade Notes Enhancements
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves urgent upgrade notes enhancements for general platform workloads and api consumers running on standard cluster nodes and runtime components, delivering operational reliability and lower maintenance toil.

high_level_changes.headline: StatefulSet PVC Auto-Cleanup, Volume Health & Storage Expansion
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves statefulset pvc auto-cleanup, volume health & storage expansion for databases, kafka/clickhouse clusters, and stateful ai checkpoint storage running on csi storage drivers and cloud block volumes, delivering eliminates orphaned cloud disk charges when scaling down or deleting temporary StatefulSets.

high_level_changes.headline: Networking, `nftables` Proxy & Traffic Observability
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves networking, `nftables` proxy & traffic observability for high-throughput east-west microservices and latency-sensitive ingress traffic running on linux dataplane (`nftables`/`ipvs`) and cloud load balancers, delivering lowers cross-AZ data transfer costs (`trafficDistribution`) and reduces node CPU spent on iptables rules.

high_level_changes.headline: CEL-Based Validating & Mutating Admission Policies
high_level_changes.plain_summary: Improves cel-based validating & mutating admission policies for platform security guardrails, multi-tenant compliance policies, and default resource injectors running on in-process `kube-apiserver` admission chain (replaces external webhook deployments), delivering removes dedicated webhook pods and eliminates deployment outages caused by webhook timeouts.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Changing a running Pod's CPU or memory requests/limits dynamically without killing and recreating the container.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Eliminates cold-start restarts and dropped connections when scaling stateful services, databases, or warm AI model servers.

jargon_glossary.meaning: An 'all-or-nothing' scheduling guarantee where a group of cooperating Pods (like a multi-node training or distributed inference job) only starts when capacity exists for the entire group.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Prevents expensive GPUs from sitting idle in deadlocked partial allocations when a cluster is near capacity.

jargon_glossary.meaning: In-process policy rules written in Common Expression Language (CEL) evaluated directly inside `kube-apiserver` without calling external admission webhook servers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Removes webhook network latency and prevents a crashed policy pod from taking down cluster deployments.

jargon_glossary.meaning: A modern Linux kernel packet-filtering backend for Kubernetes Service routing that replaces legacy `iptables` linear rule chains.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Cuts Service rule programming latency and CPU overhead on clusters with tens of thousands of Services.

jargon_glossary.meaning: Allows `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to scale external/queue-driven workloads all the way down to 0 replicas when idle and wake them when queue depth rises.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Directly cuts cloud compute and GPU bills for bursty batch/inference workers during off-peak hours.

jargon_glossary.meaning: The standard plugin layer connecting Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to cloud block/file storage providers.
jargon_glossary.why_it_matters: Controls how fast stateful workloads attach disks, recover from node failures, and handle credentials.

should_i_upgrade.text: Certificates API: * Users of the alpha certificates API should delete v1alpha1 CSRs from the API before upgrading and recreate them as v1beta1 CSR after upgrading. ([#39772](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/39772), [@mikedanese](https://github.com/mikedanese))

Cluster Autoscaler: * If you are using (or planning to use) Cluster Autoscaler please wait for Kubernetes 1.6.1. In 1.6.0 Cluster Autoscaler may occasionally increase the size of the cluster a bit more than it is actually needed, when there are unschedulable pods, scale up is required and cloud provider is slow to set up networking for new nodes. Anyway, the cluster should get back to the proper size after 10 min.

Deployment now fully respects ControllerRef to avoid fighting over Pods and ReplicaSets. At the time of upgrade, **you must not have Deployments with selectors that overlap**, or else [ownership of ReplicaSets may change](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/api-machinery/controller-ref.md#upgrading). ([#42175](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/42175), [@enisoc](https://github.com/enisoc))

Federation: * The --dns-provider argument of 'kubefed init' is now mandatory and does not default to `google-clouddns`. To initialize a Federation control plane with Google Cloud DNS, use the following invocation: 'kubefed init --dns-provider=google-clouddns' ([#42092](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/42092), [@marun](https://github.com/marun))

Federation: * Cluster federation servers have changed the location in etcd where federated services are stored, so existing federated services must be deleted and recreated. Before upgrading, export all federated services from the federation server and delete the services. After upgrading the cluster, recreate the federated services from the exported data. ([#37770](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/37770), [@enj](https://github.com/enj))
Internal Storage Layer: * upgrade to etcd3 prior to upgrading to 1.6 **OR** explicitly specify `--storage-backend=etcd2 --storage-media-type=application/json` when starting the apiserver
Node Components: * **Kubelet with the Docker-CRI implementation**
Node Components:   * The Docker-CRI implementation is enabled by default.

Node Components:   * It is not compatible with containers created by older Kubelets. It is recommended to drain your node before upgrade. If you choose to perform an in-place upgrade, the Kubelet will automatically restart all Kubernetes-managed containers on the node.

Node Components:   * It is not compatible with CNI plugins that do not conform to the [error handling behavior in the spec](https://github.com/containernetworking/cni/blob/master/SPEC.md#network-configuration-list-error-handling). The plugins are being updated to resolve this issue ([#43488](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/43488)). You can disable CRI explicitly (`--enable-cri=false`) as a temporary workaround.

This feature is beta (as the rest of taints) and enabled by default. It's gated by controller-manager enable-taint-manager flag. ([#40355](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/40355), [@gmarek](https://github.com/gmarek))

Scheduling: - **[beta]** [Node affinity/anti-affinity](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/assign-pod-node/) and **[beta]** [pod affinity/anti-affinity](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/assign-pod-node/). Node affinity/anti-affinity allow you to specify rules for restricting which node(s) a pod can schedule onto, based on the labels on the node. Pod affinity/anti-affinity allow you to specify rules for spreading and packing pods relative to one another, across arbitrary topologies (node, zone, etc.) These affinity rules are now be specified in a new-in-1.6 `affinity` field of the PodSpec. Kubernetes 1.6 continues to support the alpha `scheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/affinity` annotation on the Pod if you explicitly enable the alpha feature "AffinityInAnnotations", but it will be removed in a future release. When you upgrade to 1.6, if you have not enabled the alpha feature, then the scheduler will use the `affinity` field in PodSpec and will ignore the annotation. If you have enabled the alpha feature, then the scheduler will use the `affinity` field in PodSpec if it is present, and otherwise will use the annotation.
